_comment: Hardened seccomp profile for kojuto sandbox. Historical context — a review of PR #43 pointed out that the original ALLOW-by-default profile with 42 explicit denies made the sandbox WEAKER than Docker's stock profile because `--security-opt seccomp=<file>` REPLACES the Docker default rather than layering on top. That opened up ~300 syscalls Docker would have blocked, including io_uring which allows every kojuto detection category to be bypassed. This revision restores parity on the highest-impact gap (io_uring) while keeping ALLOW-by-default to avoid breaking legit install flows — a full deny-by-default allow-list is a maintenance liability we're deferring. memfd_create is deliberately REMOVED from the deny list so the analyzer's parseExecveat AT_EMPTY_PATH branch can catch the fileless-exec chain — inducing and observing malicious behaviour is more consistent with kojuto's design than silently blocking with ENOSYS (which also gives sandbox-aware payloads a definitive fingerprint). Because the profile is still ALLOW-by-default, the residual gap versus Docker's stock deny-by-default profile is the set of syscalls Docker blocks that are absent from the list below; the deny list now covers the ones reachable without a capability kojuto does not grant, so what remains open are calls that would EPERM against --cap-drop=ALL anyway. Any new syscall that becomes a detection-bypass or escape vector must be added here explicitly — nothing is blocked implicitly.
_archComment: archMap is REQUIRED, not cosmetic. libseccomp resolves syscall NAMES to numbers for one architecture only; a filter installed without arch coverage matches solely on the native arch (AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64). A payload that ships a static 32-bit ELF, or that issues the x32 form of a syscall (nr | 0x40000000), lands on an arch this filter has no rules for and falls straight through to defaultAction — i.e. every deny below (io_uring, mount, bpf, ptrace-attach, ...) is bypassed by recompiling for i386. Docker's stock profile carries the same archMap for exactly this reason. Entries cover kojuto's release targets (amd64, arm64); Docker selects the entry matching the host arch and adds the sub-architectures, so a host arch absent from this map degrades to the previous native-only behaviour rather than failing.

syscalls.comment: Block PTRACE_ATTACH (16). ptrace itself must stay reachable — strace is the probe — but `strace -f -- <cmd>` never uses ATTACH: it forks, the child calls PTRACE_TRACEME, and subsequent children are picked up automatically via PTRACE_O_TRACEFORK/VFORK/CLONE. ATTACH is only needed by `strace -p <pid>`, which kojuto does not run inside the container. Leaving ATTACH open let a payload attach to the strace process that is monitoring it (CAP_SYS_PTRACE bypasses the Yama ptrace_scope restriction) and stop or manipulate the tracer — an attack on monitoring integrity, not just on a sibling process. PTRACE_TRACEME (0) stays allowed so anti-debugging self-checks still execute and are reported as CategoryEvasion.

Block PTRACE_SEIZE (0x4206 = 16902) for the same reason as PTRACE_ATTACH above — it is the modern equivalent and grants the same cross-process control. Split into its own entry because the `args` list within one entry is ANDed, so two request values need two rules.

Block the bulk cross-process memory interfaces. NOTE: on its own this is NOT what makes --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE safe — PTRACE_PEEKDATA/POKEDATA read and write another process's memory without touching process_vm_*, so an earlier version of this comment (and of SECURITY.md) overstated the guarantee. The actual control is the PTRACE_ATTACH/SEIZE deny above, which removes the ability to get a handle on a process you did not fork in the first place. This rule remains as defence in depth.

Block prctl(PR_SET_NAME) specifically so an attacker cannot rename their process to `node` and bypass isV8JITPageOp. Legit Python threading.Thread(name=) and node worker_threads use this too — they will get an error return which they typically ignore (name-set is best-effort). If FP surfaces, fingerprint the caller's execve path here instead.

io_uring is the biggest detection-bypass vector kojuto had. An attacker can submit IORING_OP_OPENAT / OP_CONNECT / OP_SEND / OP_UNLINKAT via a submission-queue entry and the sys_enter_* tracepoints kojuto attaches to (strace + eBPF) will not fire because io-wq kernel workers dispatch the operations from an internal path. Docker's stock seccomp profile blocks these; the pre-hardening kojuto profile silently reopened the hole. Blocking with ERRNO forces attacker code to fall back to conventional syscalls that kojuto's probes DO observe. Sandbox-aware payloads may notice ENOSYS on io_uring_setup and pivot to declaring the environment a sandbox — that is caught separately by the CategoryEvasion rules on /proc introspection.

The pre-hardening deny list. Namespace escape (mount, umount2, pivot_root, unshare, setns, chroot); swap manipulation; host mutation (sethostname, setdomainname, reboot); kernel module loading (init/finit/delete/create_module, get_kernel_syms, query_module); kexec; eBPF; userfaultfd; perf_event_open; kernel keyring (keyctl/request_key/add_key); file handle abuse (open_by_handle_at); process comparison (kcmp); disk quota; wall-clock modification (settimeofday, clock_settime, clock_adjtime, adjtimex); nfsservctl; hardware access (ioperm, iopl, vm86, modify_ldt, personality). memfd_create is NOT in this list — see the file-level comment for the design rationale (induce + observe rather than silently block).
